Breeding colonies of the Imperial shag (Leucocarbo atriceps) are typically established on remote sub-Antarctic islands where the birds construct nests from seaweed and guano. Egg volume, a commonly used proxy for maternal investment, has been estimated at 52.6 cm³, from which the initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg is derived as 52.6 grams [Ww0 = 52.6 grams]. This value is consistent with the energetic demands of producing a relatively large egg for a cormorant of this body size. Incubation, which is shared by both parents over a period lasting approximately 26.5 days [ab = approximately 26.5 days], proceeds at a stable nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], reflecting the thermal requirements for successful embryonic development as documented by PoweAule1996. The chicks hatch covered in bare skin and rely entirely on parental brooding for thermoregulation during their first week of life, after which down feathers begin to emerge.

Fledging, a critical milestone marking the chick's ability to fly and leave the nest, occurs after a developmental interval of 45 days following hatching [tx = 45 days following hatching] at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This transition typically takes place under the active metabolic thermal conditions of the adult bird, which average 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], as sourced from DawsWhit1999. Prior to this, the nestling chick experiences a phase of rapid mass gain fueled by frequent regurgitations from both parents, who may travel considerable distances to forage at sea. The age at fledging is relatively compact for a large seabird, a pattern that may be linked to the short growing season in high-latitude environments where prey abundance peaks only briefly during the austral summer.

Sexual maturation in this species, defined by the onset of gonadal activity and the ability to produce viable gametes, does not occur until well after the chick has achieved nutritional independence. Field data indicate that puberty is attained at an age of 135 days since birth [tp = 135 days since birth], once again a period measured under the standard body temperature regime of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C] derived from DawsWhit1999. This delay ensures that growing juveniles have sufficient time to develop the physiological reserves needed for the demanding reproductive cycle. The post-fledging juvenile phase, which may last for several months, is a time of learning and refinement of foraging techniques, often involving the bird gradually gaining proficiency in diving and prey capture before it can be considered a fully competent adult.

First reproduction, representing the initiation of actual breeding behavior and the laying of the first clutch, is deferred even further than the attainment of puberty. Longitudinal studies from banded populations show that the time since birth at first brood is 511 days since birth [tR = 511 days since birth], occurring under the thermal conditions of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This protracted period between hatching and first breeding is a common life-history strategy among long-lived seabirds, where delayed maturity is traded off against higher annual survival and greater reproductive success later in life. During this pre-breeding interval, subadult birds may prospect for suitable nesting territories and occasionally engage in courtship displays without successfully producing eggs.

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in this species, with males attaining a substantially larger ultimate wet weight than females. The ultimate wet weight for females averages 2467 grams [Wwi = 2467 grams], while that for males reaches 3157 grams [Wwi = 3157 grams], a disparity of nearly 30 percent that is among the highest observed in the Phalacrocoracidae. This difference likely reflects divergent selective pressures related to male-male competition for nest sites and female choice. Despite their smaller size, females bear the greater immediate energetic cost of egg production, though both sexes invest heavily in prolonged parental care. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed as 2.8 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.8 eggs per clutch] and approximately one laying event per annual cycle, is constrained by the demands of chick rearing, with the combined effort of a breeding pair resulting in about one clutch per year [F_R_i = about one clutch per year] under the species' typical body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C]. This moderate output contributes to a maximum recorded lifespan of approximately 6497 days [am = approximately 6497 days] for individuals in the wild, a longevity that allows for multiple reproductive seasons and buffers against periodic troughs in prey availability that can cause widespread breeding failure at a temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C].
